The idea seemed simple at first: apply an external stimulus to change the shape of the cornea without cutting it. But as I went deeper, I ran into questions I could not answer. How does the cornea respond to force at a structural level? What determines whether a deformation is temporary or permanent? How can tissue be altered without causing damage or triggering scarring?

I did not have a clear way forward. Most sources either explained biology without enough detail about mechanical behavior, or focused on procedures like LASIK without unpacking the underlying physics. So I started breaking the problem down myself.

I began with the mechanical properties of the cornea, trying to understand how it behaves under stress. This led me into topics like viscoelasticity and collagen fiber networks, which I had not studied before. I read research papers, often without fully understanding them, and returned to the same sections multiple times until the assumptions started to make sense.

There were moments where progress felt almost stagnant. I remember spending a long time on a single section of a paper trying to understand how stress distribution was being modeled, only to realize I had misunderstood a basic assumption behind it. That forced me to go back and rebuild the idea from a more fundamental level instead of relying on surface interpretation.

Then I moved to how energy could be applied. I compared different methods, especially ultrasound and electromagnetic stimulation, trying to understand not just how they work, but how precisely they can be controlled. At one point, I fixated on whether a method could produce change, and ignored whether it could do so safely. That mistake forced me to shift my focus from possibility to control.

What made this process difficult was that there was no single source that connected all the pieces. I had to construct that understanding gradually, identifying where ideas aligned, where they conflicted, and where assumptions broke down.

The one idea in the world of science, logic, and math that interests me greatly is the idea of cause and effect. It seems simply wonderful how even the smallest event can trigger the biggest of changes. This is very well explained through the concept of feedback loops and chain reactions.

In a chain reaction, each event becomes the cause of the next reaction, and it is already the effect of the previous one. This "domino effect," so to speak, is one of the most interesting phenomena in the environment. But this is a chain that moves forward and stops only when it runs out of "fuel," which, in this case, is energy.

In a feedback loop, however, the cause-and-effect chain is more circular in nature. This is even more interesting, as it sometimes even acts as a self-correcting system. For example, if the cause is feeling too hot, the effect will be sweating, which immediately works against the cause. However, there is also a positive loop where the effect adds to the cause. For example, if the cause is a microphone picking up sound, the effect is the speaker playing it louder. It is a self-reinforcing cycle.

Section G - Essay Curiosity:
It started as a standard school science project, find a problem, propose a solution, make it look good on chart paper, so I picked plastic waste because it seemed interesting. And then I found PHB, and something shifted.

PHB is a bioplastic that actually competes with petroleum plastic, in strength, heat resistance, water resistance, and biodegradability. Nearly perfect. Except it costs ₹3,500 per kilogram while regular plastic costs almost nothing. I wanted to know why.

So I started reading. Not textbooks, research papers. I read many research papers available on ScienceDirect, PubMed, MDPI related to PHB, its production and distribution and market. I learned that 70-80% of PHB's production cost comes from its feedstock: refined sugars fed to a bacterium called Cupriavidus necator. I thought: what if we replace refined sugars with something we'd otherwise throw away?

That's how algae entered the picture. Algal blooms destroy aquatic ecosystems and cost governments crores to clean up. Using that biomass as feedstock feels elegant; it solves two problems with one process. I won first place at the state level with that idea.

Then I actually stress-tested it.

Preparing for nationals, I went back to the papers. I found something uncomfortable: cyanobacteria — the algae in algal blooms — are high in nitrogen and phosphorus. PHB production in C. necator requires a nitrogen-deficient environment in Stage 2. Too much nitrogen and the bacteria never switch from growing to producing. My core idea had a structural flaw.

I sat with that for a while. Then I looked at agricultural wet waste — sugarcane molasses, bagasse, fruit pulp. Low nitrogen, rich in carbon. Good yields. But I'd already named my project around algae and couldn't abandon it entirely.

That constraint forced a better idea. What if both were used together — algae providing the nutrient density for explosive bacterial growth in Stage 1, and bagasse-molasses taking over in Stage 2 when nitrogen needs to run out? I calculated a 4:3 algae-to-molasses ratio for Stage 1 and a 2:1 bagasse-to-molasses ratio for Stage 2. The projected yields were 65-80% of cell dry weight, higher than either feedstock alone.

I called it SuperMix.

I also redesigned the extraction process, replacing chloroform with 0.3M NaOH at 30°C, achieving 99.8% purity in literature, and building two tracks: a faster, cheaper route for commercial PHB and a high-purity route for medical use.

The projected industrial cost: ₹44-113 per kilogram versus ₹3,500 currently imported.

What I learned isn't just biochemistry. It's that the first version of an idea is never the real idea, it's just the door. Every paper I read opened a new problem, and every problem forced a more honest solution.
Section G - Essay Motivation:
So after I finished my thermodynamics chapter my feed was filled with similar things and I stumbled across a thought experiment which challenges the 2nd law of thermodynamics, i watched that short video and went on to know more about it.

Maxwell's Demon. An 1867 thought experiment that nearly broke physics.

A simple setup, a box of gas, two chambers, one tiny door. A demon sits there sorting molecules. Fast ones in the right chamber, and slow ones in left. One side heats up, the other cools down which creates a temperature difference for free without any work done. And with this hypothetical situation he just violated the second law, entropy decreased.

For a century, nobody could debunk this properly.

Then Landauer cracked it. He suggested that the demon has to remember every molecule it sees. And memory isn't free, when it erases that information, it dumps heat into the environment. Exactly enough heat to compensate and with this the second law survives.

This means information is physical. Erasing one bit of data has a measurable thermodynamic cost.

So everything I studied, entropy, irreversibility, heat engines, it all secretly connected to computation and information theory.

Learning how everyday devices work has always been interesting to me, particularly something as common as charging a mobile phone. One day, I became curious about how the electricity from the wall socket known as alternating current (AC) mains is able to charge a mobile phone battery, which actually works on direct current (DC) based charging. This question motivated me to explore and understand the science behind it on my own.
At first, I only knew that the electricity in our homes is AC, meaning it alternates between positive values and negative values many a times per second like a graph of sinusoidal function. On the other hand, a mobile phone battery works with either positive value or negative value without alternating with time. This difference made me wonder: how does my phone safely charge when the types of current are different in the AC mains and battery?
To find the answer, I started researching online and watching educational videos. I learned that the charger we use is not just a simple connector but a small electronic device that performs an important function. Inside the charger, there is a component called a rectifier. The rectifier converts AC into DC by allowing current to flow in only one direction. This process is called rectification.
But the process does not stop there. I also discovered that the current from the wall is at a much higher voltage (around 220V in India), which is too strong for a mobile phone battery. So, the charger also contains a transformer that reduces the voltage to a much safer level. After that, the current is smoothed using filters so that it becomes steady DC, suitable for charging the battery.
Another important thing I learned is that mobile phones have a built-in charging circuit. This circuit ensures that the battery charges safely by controlling the amount of current entering the battery. It prevents overcharging, which could otherwise damage the battery or reduce its lifespan.
Through this self-learning experience, I understood that charging a phone is not as simple as just plugging it in. It involves several steps: converting AC to DC, reducing voltage, and regulating current. This made me appreciate the role of science and engineering in our daily lives.
This experience also taught me the importance of curiosity and self-learning. By asking a simple question and trying to find the answer myself, I gained valuable knowledge. It showed me that learning does not always require a classroom; sometimes, real understanding comes from observing everyday life and exploring it deeply.
In conclusion, learning how AC current is converted to DC to charge a mobile battery was both interesting and useful. It not only increased my knowledge of basic electronics but also encouraged me to keep questioning and learning new things independently.

There are many ideas in science that I find interesting, but the one that has stayed with me most is the EPR paradox. What pulled me toward it was the fact that it did not feel like an ordinary physics concept. It felt like a serious question about how reality actually works.

Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen proposed this paradox because they felt quantum mechanics did not tell the whole story. They imagined two particles that interacted and then drifted far apart. In quantum theory, some of their properties are not fixed before measurement. Yet once one particle is measured, the state of the other becomes clear at once. Einstein found this troubling. To him, it meant either the particles carried hidden information all along or that measurement involved a strange link across distance.

What I find most interesting about the EPR paradox is that it is convincing and unsettling at the same time. It begins with physics, but it leads to a much deeper question about what is actually real. That is why it stayed with me. It made me feel that science becomes most exciting when it forces us to rethink what we thought was obvious.

Intellectual curiosity is often mistakenly confined to the sterile environment of classrooms and standardized exams. We are frequently taught to view learning as a simple transaction: memorize this theory, analyze this text, remember this historical date, and in return, receive a passing grade. But true intellectual curiosity is a far wilder, more untamed force. It is the quiet, relentless itch in the back of the mind that refuses to accept the world at face value. It is the fundamental rebellion against the "default settings" of our lives, driving us to dismantle the reality around us just to see how the underlying mechanisms interlock.
At its core, this curiosity is driven by an insatiable desire to understand the human condition. It is what compels a mind to look beyond the surface of a classic text, not merely to admire the prose, but to dissect the profound sociological currents running beneath it. The deeply curious mind understands that narratives and society are mirrors reflecting one another. The same analytical rigor required to deconstruct a canonical piece of literature is the exact same mental muscle used to untangle the complex power dynamics, institutional structures, and unwritten rules that govern our everyday interactions. Everything is a story waiting to be interpreted.
To be intellectually curious is to embrace the profound discomfort of ignorance. It is the willingness to stare at a dense, seemingly impenetrable philosophy or a complex societal issue and say, "I do not understand this yet, but I will." This journey inherently involves falling down endless rabbit holes. It means spending hours researching the historical context of a single movement—not because it is required for an assessment, but because the brain demands resolution. It is the thrill of connecting an abstract theoretical framework to a fleeting observation on a bustling city street, suddenly seeing the invisible threads that dictate human behavior.
Furthermore, this kind of curiosity is inherently active, never passive. It demands that we question, critique, and synthesize. It is the refusal to accept a system or a paradigm exactly as it is presented by authority. When we ask, "Whose voice is missing from this narrative?" or "Why is this foundation structured this way?", we shift from being mere consumers of culture to active participants in its evolution. This drive for deeper understanding stems from a fundamental belief that the world is malleable and that rigorous knowledge is the tool required to shape it.
Ultimately, intellectual curiosity is the engine of a deeply lived life. It insulates us against boredom, apathy, and dogma. When the world is viewed through the lens of relentless inquiry, nothing is ever truly mundane. Every conversation, every piece of art, and every societal shift becomes a vital piece in the grand, ongoing project of understanding who we are and why we build the realities we do. It is a lifelong commitment to asking "why," a commitment that transforms the ordinary into an endless landscape of discovery.

​Instead of a simple drug delivery, my system uses an Engineered EColi bacteria as 5-payload vector controlled by an 'If-Else' logic circuit. This If-Else circuitry ensures that the system remains dormant in healthy tissue, where conditions fail the logic check. By requiring simultaneous activation of both 'locks' before releasing the 5-payload delivery, the chassis minimizes off-target toxicity and ensures localized treatment.

Over the past few months, I have been self-studying "The Elements of Computing Systems," building a 16-bit computer (the "Hack" platform) from first principles. This journey through layers of abstraction—from NAND gates to a functioning CPU—has provided a profound perspective on how hardware realises logic.

The most significant challenge has been implementing the 16-bit ALU and Program Counter (PC). For the ALU, I avoided the "sign-bit" shortcut to strictly adhere to the constraint of preventing "negative zero" issues as mentioned in the book. To overcome this, I developed a logic-based solution: adding half the binary capacity to the output and monitoring the carry bit for an overflow. If the carry bit was zero, we are sure the number was positive, since half the capacity would overflow if it were negative, per our convention. To the computer, it would still be anomalous—this logically verified negativity without relying on simple MSB extraction. Similarly, for the PC, I implemented a hierarchical logic chain—increment, then load, then reset—to ensure the reset bit maintains absolute priority in the sequential logic.

My journey has also taught me that what is omitted in hardware can be optimized in software. By implementing addition using XOR, we get subtraction for "free" using 2's complement. While implementing multiplication in Assembly (.asm), I tried to develop a cycle-efficient heuristic: the program compares the two operands and selects the smaller value as the loop counter. For a calculation like 1 x 12,345, my implementation ensures the larger value is added once rather than performing 12,345 iterations. I was a little proud of this achievement as I thought reducing the ALU cycles might result in performance gains. 

My commitment to low-level engineering began with a school project: a mock CoWin portal in Python. While it was selected for a showcase, I was unsatisfied with the high-level abstractions and the "Maximum Recursion Depth" limits I encountered. Stability of the atomic nucleus, despite the strong repulsion between positively charged protons, is one of the most fascinating scientific ideas to me. According to electrostatics, these protons should push each other apart, making the nucleus unstable. Yet atoms exist in a stable form, suggesting the presence of a force that overcomes this electrostatic repulsion. This force is the strong nuclear force, which acts between nucleons (protons and neutrons). It is extremely powerful but operates only over very short distances, about 1–3 femtometers, allowing it to dominate when nucleons are very close.

Essay: My Journey with the Keys

Intellectual curiosity, to me, isn’t about winning a science fair or reading a giant encyclopedia. It is that tiny itch in your brain that makes you want to figure something out just because you can. For me, that itch started last summer when I decided I wanted to learn how to play the piano. We had an old electronic keyboard gathering dust in the corner of the living room, and one afternoon, I simply decided I was tired of just looking at it.

The problem was that I had no teacher, no books, and absolutely no idea where to start. To be honest, looking at the long row of black and white keys was intimidating. They all looked exactly the same to me. However, instead of giving up, I turned to the one place where I knew I could find help: YouTube. 

I began searching for "piano for absolute beginners." While the videos were helpful, I struggled to remember which key was which. The instructors kept talking about ‘C Major’ or ‘F Sharp,’ but by the time I looked down at my hands, I was lost. That is when I came up with a simple, DIY solution. I took some masking tape and a black marker. I labeled each white key with its corresponding letter—A, B, C, D, and so on. 

Some people might say that marking the keys is "cheating," but for a self-learner like me, it was a roadmap. It allowed me to bridge the gap between the video on my screen and the instrument under my fingers. I spent hours every evening in front of that keyboard. I would watch a five-second clip of a song, pause it, find the letters on my marked keys, and play it back. 

At first, it sounded terrible. My rhythm was off, and my fingers felt stiff and clumsy. There were moments of real frustration when I couldn't get my left hand to cooperate with my right hand. But because I was learning for myself—not for a grade or an exam—I didn't feel the pressure to be perfect. I just felt curious to see if I could finish one full song. 

After about three weeks of practice, I finally played a simplified version of "Harry potter tune" without stopping. The feeling of accomplishment was incredible. Eventually, I became so familiar with the positions that I was able to peel the tape off the keys. I didn’t need the labels anymore; the music was in my head.

This experience taught me that learning isn't always about being in a classroom. It’s about being resourceful. I learned that if you have a bit of patience and a YouTube connection, you can teach yourself almost anything. Most importantly, I realized that "intellectual curiosity" is just a fancy way of saying that you're willing to try, fail, and try again until the music sounds .

A great and simple science idea is to create a Density Tower, which demonstrates how different liquids have different densities (how compact or "heavy" they are).
The Density Tower Experiment
Concept: Liquids with higher density sink to the bottom, while less dense liquids float on top.
Materials: Honey, dish soap, water (colored with food dye), vegetable oil, rubbing alcohol, and a tall, clear glass.
Procedure: Carefully pour the liquids into the glass one by one in this order: Honey, Dish Soap, Water, Oil, and Rubbing Alcohol.
Result: Instead of mixing, the liquids will form distinct, colorful layers.
Why it works: The heavier, more dense liquids stay at the bottom, while the lighter, less dense liquids float.
Variation: You can drop a bolt (sinks), cherry tomato (floats on soap), and ping-pong ball (floats on oil) into the tower to see how they settle in the different layers based on their own densities.

Section G - Essay Curiosity:
As a child, I watched my cousins build machinga vandi in our courtyard in Kerala. Their small cars, made from two baby coconuts, a jackfruit leaf, and coconut leaf midribs called eerkil, rolled forward with ease. When I tried to build one myself, it failed almost immediately. It tilted, stalled, or collapsed. Watching was not enough. I had to figure it out on my own.

My first instinct was imitation. I copied what I had seen as closely as I could. But small differences produced completely different results. When the coconuts were not equal in size, the car leaned and dragged instead of rolling forward. When the eerkil were too thin, they bent under the load. When they were too thick, they restricted motion. The jackfruit leaf had to support the structure without tearing, which meant it needed both flexibility and strength.

Movement was even more puzzling. Some versions of the car moved a short distance and stopped. Others refused to move at all. I began testing surfaces without realizing it. On rough ground, the car slowed almost instantly. On smoother ground, it travelled farther with the same initial push. I adjusted the placement of the eerkil and noticed that even slight misalignment caused the wheels to resist each other. The car would wobble or veer instead of moving straight. I was observing friction, alignment, and resistance, even though I did not yet have the language for them.

Failure did not discourage me. It narrowed my focus. Each unsuccessful attempt became a question. Why did this version collapse? Why did that one turn? Why did another move farther? I started making deliberate changes instead of random ones. I chose coconuts more carefully to match their size. I tested different thicknesses of eerkil. I adjusted angles and spacing. With each modification, I was isolating variables without knowing the term. The process was slow, but it was precise.

What began as imitation became investigation. I was no longer trying to recreate what my cousins had built. I was trying to understand the conditions that made it work. Over time, the car improved, but more importantly, my approach changed. I began to expect failure as part of the process. Each result, whether successful or not, carried information.

Years later, when I encountered scientific concepts in a classroom, they felt familiar. Friction explained the resistance I had observed on rough surfaces. Symmetry and balance explained why equal-sized wheels mattered. Structural stability explained why certain combinations of materials held while others failed. These weren't new ideas. They were explanations for patterns I had already explored.

This was the first time I truly learned something on my own. There were no instructions, no corrections, and no clear endpoint. There was only curiosity and the need to resolve it. That experience shaped how I approach learning even now. I observe closely, question outcomes, and refine my understanding through repeated attempts.

I began by watching. I continued by questioning. I learned by refusing to stop at not knowing.

Intellectual curiosity is the desire to learn, question, and understand how things work in a deeper way. It encourages people to explore new ideas and find solutions to real-world problems. At first glance, water seems like an ideal fuel because it is abundant and environmentally friendly. However, water (H₂O) is already a stable compound, which means it does not release energy easily. To use water as a source of energy, it must first be broken down into its components—hydrogen and oxygen. This process is called electrolysis, where electricity is passed through water to separate hydrogen gas (H₂) and oxygen gas (O₂).

The hydrogen obtained from this process can be used as a fuel. In hydrogen fuel cell vehicles, hydrogen reacts with oxygen in a controlled way to produce electricity. This process is based on a chemical reaction where hydrogen atoms lose electrons and combine with oxygen to form water again. The energy released during this reaction is converted into electrical energy, which powers the vehicle’s motor. The only byproduct is water vapor, making it a clean and eco-friendly technology.

Another important scientific concept involved is energy conversion. To split water into hydrogen and oxygen, energy is required, usually in the form of electricity. If this electricity comes from renewable sources like solar or wind energy, the entire process becomes sustainable. However, if fossil fuels are used to generate this electricity, the environmental benefits are reduced. This shows that while the idea of “vehicles running on water” is attractive, the complete system must be considered.

Intellectual curiosity drives scientists and engineers to improve these technologies. They work on making electrolysis more efficient, storing hydrogen safely, and designing better fuel cells. For example, hydrogen is a very light and flammable gas, so it must be stored under high pressure or in special materials. These challenges require continuous research and innovation.

This topic also highlights the importance of questioning and critical thinking. Instead of simply believing that cars can run directly on water, curious minds explore the science behind it. They learn about chemical reactions, energy transformations, and environmental impact. This deeper understanding helps in making realistic and practical advancements.

In Aquaponics fish are kept in tanks and regularly fed their appropriate diet, the fish excrete waste (which contain nutrients) into their surroundings, the water in the tank is regularly rotated with the help of pumps and the harmful wastes in the water are filtered out leaving only nutrient rich water. This water is then led into a floating grid which contain green leafy plants that have their roots free in the water. When the nutrients in the water are used up by the plants, it is transported back into the fish lake for a closed loop.This saves water, rears healthy fish & grow plants without requiring soil.

Some of the drawbacks to Aquaponics are- Reliance on large supply of electricity for pumps, very high initial costs for setting up infrastructure, constant maintenance & careful care of the fishes. In my model, a metal disc is attached to a rotating motor. When the disc rotates freely, it keeps moving due to inertia. We began with a clear plan: use gas sensors to measure environmental conditions and display the readings. After learning how these sensors function—how gas concentration affects electrical resistance—we expected the system to behave predictably but it didn’t.

Even in what seemed like stable conditions, the readings fluctuated. Numbers shifted without any obvious reason. At first, we assumed there must be an error—either in the code or the circuit. We spent time debugging, rechecking connections, and simplifying the program. But the inconsistencies remained.

What stayed with me was the moment we realized that the issue might not be a mistake—it might be the nature of the system itself.

That realization changed how I approached the project. While we continued working together to refine the setup, I became particularly interested in understanding why the data behaved this way. I began reading more about how low cost gas sensors respond to environmental variables like humidity and temperature, and how they often lack precise selectivity. What we had been treating as a direct measurement was actually a composite signal influenced by multiple factors.

This shifted our approach. Instead of trying to extract a single “correct” value, we began looking at patterns over time. I experimented with simple filtering techniques to reduce noise and explored basic calibration methods, while we discussed how to make the system more consistent overall. Even then, it was clear that uncertainty could not be completely removed.

There were moments when the lack of clear answers was frustrating. Progress felt slow and it would have been easier to simplify the system and ignore these complications. But I found myself more engaged because of the uncertainty, not despite it.

I also began thinking about how the data would actually be used. If the readings were imperfect, how could they still be meaningful? I worked on presenting trends rather than exact values, so that the system reflected variability instead of hiding it. This required me to think not just as someone building the system, but as someone interpreting it.

Looking back, what stayed with me was not just the outcome, but the shift in how I thought about problems. Working in a team meant that we could test ideas, challenge assumptions and approach the same issue from different angles. At the same time, it pushed me to independently explore questions that did not have immediate answers.

I learned that understanding often begins when expectations fail and that uncertainty is not something to avoid, but something to work with. This experience made me more comfortable with open ended problems—where there is no single correct answer, only better ways of thinking about the question.

With more confidence, I built my second robot, The Mud-Skipper. This was a robust machine designed for speed in typical roboraces. It performed beautifully on flat ground, but I made a classic beginner’s mistake: I equipped it with sleek on-road wheels. When it faced the steep obstacles of a real track, it couldn't grip. It failed to climb, and I watched my hard work stall out. It was a frustrating lesson in physics, but it taught me that a robot is only as good as its wheels.

The National Stage: Titan-Bolt
My third and most advanced robot was Titan-Bolt, a high-speed line follower. When I first took it to a competition, I wasn't even thinking about winning. For example, when working with f(x) = x^2, I expanded (x + h)^2 into x^2 + 2xh + h^2, substituted it back, and simplified the expression step by step. Observing how the h^2 term becomes insignificant as h becomes very small helped me understand that the derivative emerges from local linear behavior.

I then tested this framework on less straightforward cases. In implicit differentiation, such as x^2 + y^2 = 1, I initially treated y as independent and made errors. Correcting this forced me to think of y as a function of x and apply the chain rule consistently. I also explored and understood the derivations of trigonometric functions.

To push this further, I moved to problems where the structure was less obvious and required careful setup. For example, I worked with functions like f(x) = |x|, where the usual differentiation rules do not apply clearly at every point. By going back to the definition (f(x + h) − f(x)) / h and evaluating the limit from both sides, I saw that the derivative behaves differently depending on the direction of approach, and fails to exist at x = 0. This was one of the first times I understood that differentiability is also dependent on other conditions.

I also explored functions like f(x) = x^(1/3), where the derivative becomes unbounded near x = 0. Working through the limit definition here showed me how the slope does not simply “fail to exist,” but instead diverges. Similarly, I looked at oscillatory functions where the function is continuous at x = 0 but behaves irregularly in every neighborhood around it.

For integration, I deliberately chose functions where standard antiderivatives do not exist in elementary form. For example, I looked at the integral of e^(−x^2) over an interval. Section G - Essay Curiosity:
At some point during my Lumiere research I hit a wall. My EEG classification model was producing results that were technically fine but not good enough. The features I was extracting using standard approaches were noisy and I could tell something was off, I just did not know what.

I went down a rabbit hole trying to figure out better feature selection. I came across the Boruta algorithm completely by accident, through a random Stack Overflow thread at around midnight. Boruta is named after a Slavic forest demon, which honestly made me trust it immediately. The idea behind it is clever in a slightly chaotic way. It creates shadow copies of your features, shuffles them randomly, and then checks whether your real features are doing better than the shuffled fake ones. If they are not, it throws them out. It is basically a method that works by figuring out what does not matter.

I had no idea if it would work for EEG data. It was not something my mentor suggested. I just thought it was interesting and decided to try it. I spent a few days reading the original research paper, watching explanations on YouTube, and then just implementing it myself in Python using the BorutaPy library and testing it against my existing pipeline.
It worked. The feature set it produced was cleaner and the model performance improved noticeably. I ended up building that finding into my research paper as one of the methodological contributions.

That experience taught me something I did not expect. The best thing I found during that entire research project was not something I was assigned to find. It came from being genuinely curious at midnight about a feature selection algorithm named after a demon.

I think that is the honest version of what self directed learning looks like most of the time. It is not structured or particularly efficient. It is following something that sounds interesting, going three tabs too deep, losing track of time, and occasionally stumbling onto something that actually matters. Most of the time it leads nowhere. That one time it did and it changed the whole direction of my research.

Since then I have tried to keep that habit. I will read about something completely unrelated to whatever I am working on just because it caught my attention. Sometimes it connects back in ways I did not expect. Most of the time it does not and I just know a random thing about forest demons or signal processing or the history of neural networks that nobody asked me to know.
I think that kind of curiosity, the kind that does not need a reason or a grade attached to it, is the most useful thing I have developed. It is what led me to the Boruta algorithm, to EEG research, to AI development, and honestly to most things I am proud of.

After going outside of the school curriculum , i learnt that it turns out that multiplying with iota (i)  is, from the argand plane perspective, a 90 degree rotation. Project OXCART: Breaking the Sound Barrier in Simulation

Driven by a lifelong fascination with military aviation and fifth-generation fighters like the F-22 Raptor, I decided to spend my transition break between Class 11 and Class 12 diving deep into the world of aerospace engineering. My goal was simple but ambitious: to design, simulate, and optimize a high-performance rocket capable of supersonic speeds using OpenRocket software. I named this endeavor "Project OXCART," a tribute to the Lockheed A-12 and the legendary engineering spirit of Kelly Johnson. What followed was an intense three-day technical marathon that pushed my understanding of physics and design to its limits.

The first day was dedicated to Prototype-1 (Proto-1). For this initial model, I opted for a classic ogive nose cone geometry, which is excellent for subsonic and low-transonic efficiency. I spent hours tweaking the center of gravity and center of pressure to ensure the rocket wouldn't tumble mid-flight. By the end of day one, Proto-1 was a success, reaching a top speed of Mach 0.919. While I was proud of this result, I knew I hadn't yet crossed the most significant threshold in aviation: the sound barrier.

Day two turned into a complete nightmare. Transitioning from transonic to supersonic speeds isn't just about adding more power; it’s about completely rethinking fluid dynamics. As I pushed for higher velocities, my simulations began showing massive stability failures and "drag-burn" issues. I spent the entire second day fighting with the physics of air resistance. The drag caused by the standard four-fin setup was too high, and the ogive nose was no longer efficient at these speeds. I had to manually recalculate the cross-section of the rocket to reduce its frontal area, essentially "slimming down" the entire airframe to minimize the air it had to displace.

By the morning of the third day, after dozens of failed iterations, I finally found the winning configuration for Prototype-2. First, I elongated the body tube to improve the fineness ratio. I replaced the ogive nose with a Power Series geometry, which is significantly more effective at Mach speeds exceeding the speed of sound. To handle the increased structural stress, I switched the material selection to carbon fiber for its incredible strength-to-weight ratio.

The most radical change, however,  the stabilization system. To cut down on parasitic drag, I removed the traditional four-fin layout and installed a single set of three smaller fins. This reduced the surface area exposed to the wind while still maintaining the necessary stability. I paired this streamlined frame with a much more powerful solid rocket motor. The result was a breakthrough: Prototype-2 successfully hit Mach 1.48.

This three-day project was more than just a simulation; it was a practical lesson in iterative design. It taught me that engineering is rarely about getting it right the first time—it's about the grit required on "Day Two" when nothing is working. Achieving supersonic flight, even in a digital environment, gave me a profound respect for the complexity of the aircraft I’ve always admired.

The Aerofoil: Mastering Lift and Flow
An aerofoil (or airfoil) is a cross-sectional shape designed to generate a functional aerodynamic force when moved through a fluid. Primarily found in aircraft wings, turbine blades, and sails, its geometry is the cornerstone of modern flight.
Geometry and Design
The effectiveness of an aerofoil is defined by its specific anatomy. Key parameters include the Leading Edge (the front point that meets the air), the Trailing Edge (the sharp rear point), and the Chord Line—an imaginary straight line connecting the two. The Camber represents the asymmetry between the upper and lower surfaces, which significantly influences the lift-to-drag ratio.
Physics of Lift
The generation of lift is best explained through two complementary principles of physics:
Bernoulli’s Principle: Due to the aerofoil’s curvature, air typically travels faster over the top surface than the bottom. According to Bernoulli’s equation, this increase in velocity results in a decrease in pressure, creating a "suction" effect that pulls the wing upward.
Newton’s Third Law: As the aerofoil moves, it deflects the incoming air downwards (downwash). The reaction to this downward momentum change is an equal and opposite upward force: Lift.
Optimized aerofoil  design maximize life and efficiency to prevent aerodynamicstall

*The Power of Catalysis: Accelerating Chemical Reactions*

Catalysis is a fundamental concept in chemistry that has revolutionized the way we live and interact with the world around us. A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed or permanently altered in the process. This remarkable ability has made catalysis a crucial component in many industrial processes, from the production of fuels and chemicals to the reduction of environmental pollutants.

*How Catalysis Works*

A catalyst works by lowering the activation energy required for a reaction to occur. This allows the reaction to proceed faster and more efficiently, often at lower temperatures and pressures. The catalyst achieves this by providing an alternative reaction pathway, often involving the formation of intermediate complexes with the reactants.

*Types of Catalysis*

There are several types of catalysis, including:

- *Homogeneous catalysis*: The catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants, often a liquid or gas.
- *Heterogeneous catalysis*: The catalyst is in a different phase, often a solid, while the reactants are gases or liquids.
- *Enzymatic catalysis*: Biological molecules, such as enzymes, act as catalysts in living organisms.

*Applications of Catalysis*

Catalysis has numerous applications across various industries:

- *Fuel production*: Catalysis is used to convert crude oil into fuels, such as gasoline and diesel.
- *Chemical synthesis*: Catalysis is used to produce many chemicals, including fertilizers, plastics, and pharmaceuticals.
- *Environmental protection*: Catalysis is used to reduce emissions from vehicles and industrial processes, converting pollutants into harmless gases.
- *Pharmaceuticals*: Catalysis is used to synthesize complex molecules, such as antibiotics and anticancer drugs.

The Speed of Light: My Journey into Li-Fi
The concept of the "spectrum crunch" first drew me in—the idea that our global appetite for data is outstripping the capacity of invisible radio waves. While most see a desk lamp as a simple tool for illumination, I became obsessed with the idea that it could be a conduit for high-speed internet. This curiosity led me to spend months teaching myself the mechanics of Li-Fi (Light Fidelity), a technology that uses the visible light spectrum to transmit data.
My journey began not in a classroom, but in the depths of research papers and hardware forums. I wanted to understand how a standard LED could be modulated—flickered millions of times per second—to encode binary data without the human eye ever perceiving a change. To a beginner, the physics was daunting: I had to grasp the relationship between photonics and digital signal processing. Without a formal mentor, I turned to open-source communities and technical documentation to map out a prototype.
The construction phase was a lesson in persistence. My initial setup was humble: an Arduino microcontroller, a high-power LED as the transmitter, and a small solar panel acting as the receiver. The "The How" was a series of grueling trials. My first major hurdle was "noise." In a room filled with ambient sunlight and overhead fluorescent bulbs, my photodiode was overwhelmed. The signal-to-noise ratio was so poor that my receiver couldn’t distinguish between the data stream and the room’s lighting.
Instead of giving up, I dove into signal filtering. I taught myself how to implement a simple hardware-based high-pass filter to block out the steady DC offset of ambient light. I spent hours realigning the transmitter and receiver, learning the hard way about the strict "line-of-sight" requirements of optical wireless communication. When I finally successfully transmitted a simple string of text—a "Hello World" sent via a beam of light—the satisfaction wasn't just in the working circuit; it was in the realization that I had engineered a solution to a problem I barely understood weeks prior.
This project shifted my perspective on innovation. It taught me that groundbreaking technology doesn’t always require entirely new infrastructure; sometimes, it requires reimagining what we already have. Beyond the technical skills—soldering, C++ coding for the Arduino, and basic circuit design—I discovered my own capacity for self-directed learning. I learned how to sit with a problem, break it into its physics-based components, and iterate until a solution emerged.
Intellectual curiosity, I’ve found, is the willingness to follow a "what if" into the unknown. My Li-Fi project was more than a weekend experiment; it was a proof of concept for my future academic career. It proved that when I am faced with a complex, multi-layered problem, I have the resourcefulness to illuminate my own path toward an answer.

It was the middle of the monsoon when our internet went down for almost two weeks. There were no online classes, no YouTube, and no distractions. Just rain, boredom, and an old wooden chess set collecting dust on top of our bookshelf. I had never played seriously before. I knew how the pieces moved in strange ways, and that was about it. With nothing else to do, I pulled it down, wiped off the dust, and decided to teach myself how to play.

The first few days were messy. I kept losing to my father in fewer than ten moves. He would smile, reset the board, and say, "Try again." I tried again, and again. Each loss felt worse than the last. I started to feel stupid, honestly, like maybe chess just wasn’t for me. But something about the quiet click of the pieces on the board kept drawing me back.

So I stopped playing randomly and started thinking. I borrowed an old, yellowing chess book from my neighbor, the kind with tiny diagrams and long Russian names I could barely pronounce. I read it slowly, sometimes going over the same page three or four times. I began noticing things I had never seen before—how a knight could fork two pieces at once, how pawns could become powerful if pushed together, and how the center of the board mattered more than the edges. It felt like the game had a hidden language, and I was finally learning its alphabet.

I practiced alone for hours. I played against myself, switching sides and arguing in my head like two different people. The rain outside became background music to my small battles. Some nights, I dreamed of chess moves. My mother thought I had lost it.

Then one evening, I beat my father. Not by luck, but with a plan I had carefully thought through. He stared at the board, laughed, and said, "Beta, now I have to study too." That moment felt bigger than any exam result.

Looking back, chess did not just teach me a game. It taught me how to lose without breaking, how to think before reacting, and how silence can sometimes be the best teacher. Nobody forced me to learn it. That’s what made it matter. And somewhere between the rain and the rooks, I think I grew up a little.

The YUVIKA program at ISRO was a turning point for me, specifically the day we were tasked with building a functional rover from a kit of motors, sensors, and structural beams. The project wasn't just about making a "car"; it was about understanding how a machine survives in an environment where there are no roads.

We began with the mechanical assembly, which was far more complex than it appeared on paper. The core of our design was the rocker-bogie suspension system, the same mechanism used by  ISRO’s Pragyan rovers. This system involves two arms with a pivot point, allowing the chassis to climb obstacles twice the diameter of the wheels while keeping all six wheels in constant contact with the ground. Assembling the linkages required precise measurements; even a millimeter of misalignment meant the rover would "crab-walk" or veer off-course. We spent hours tightening bolts and ensuring the joints moved fluidly, creating a skeleton that could theoretically endure the rugged lunar terrain.

Once the physical frame was solid, we transitioned to the electronic integration. This involved mounting four high-torque DC motors to the wheels and connecting them to an L298N motor driver and an Arduino microcontroller. We had to carefully route the wiring through the chassis to ensure that the movement of the suspension wouldn't snag or snap the cables. It was a delicate balancing act of managing cable slack while maintaining a clean, professional layout.

However, the real drama began during the first power-up. When I uploaded the code and activated the battery pack, the rover didn't glide forward as expected. Instead, it stayed rooted to the spot, performing frantic rotatory motion. The wheels were screaming, and the chassis was vibrating violently, pivoting around its central axis like a spinning top. No matter how much we adjusted the code or repositioned the weight, we could achieve no translatory motion. We had over-analyzed the problem. We checked the friction of the tires and wondered if the center of gravity was too high, causing the wheels to lose traction. We spent an hour recalibrating the motor speeds in the software. But the breakthrough came when I took a multimeter to the wiring harness.

I discovered that the error wasn't in the physics or the code, but in a single wire connection. In our rush to finish the assembly, we had reversed the polarity of the wires on the right-side motors. While the left side was receiving a signal to move "forward," the right side was receiving a "reverse" signal. By simply swapping those two wires, we aligned the phase of all four motors.

When I flipped the switch for the second time, the transformation was magic. The spinning stopped, and the rover surged forward with a steady, purposeful crawl. It handled the simulated rock field with ease, the rocker-bogie arms tilting and dipping to absorb the uneven ground. This taught me a vital lesson in engineering: even the most complex mechanical structure is useless if the underlying electronic logic is flawed.

I remember one night when I was looking at the sky and a simple question came to my mind: if there are billions of stars in the universe, why is the night sky dark? At first, it felt like a childish doubt, something too obvious to question. But the more I thought about it, the more it started to bother me. If stars are spread out everywhere, then in every direction we look, our line of sight should eventually hit a star. In that case, the entire sky should glow brightly, almost like the surface of the Sun. But clearly, that is not what we see.
This curiosity led me to discover something called Olbers’ Paradox. It explains this exact contradiction between what we expect and what we actually observe. What fascinated me most was not just the answer, but how such a simple question could challenge our understanding of the universe itself. As I explored further, I realized that the darkness of the night sky is actually evidence that the universe is not infinite in age. Since light takes time to travel, we can only see stars whose light has had enough time to reach us. There are many regions of the universe whose light simply hasn’t arrived yet.
I also learned that the universe is expanding, which means distant stars and galaxies are moving away from us. Because of this, their light gets stretched and loses energy, sometimes shifting out of the visible range entirely. So even though those stars exist, we cannot see them in the night sky.
What started as a small doubt turned into something much bigger. It made me realize that science often begins with very ordinary questions, but the answers can reveal extraordinary truths. We were learning about plants and their different mechanisms for carrying out their life processes under a chapter called "Getting To Know Plants". Basically the topic was about the transportation of water and minerals by xylem vessels present in the lower parts of the plant to the upper parts for carrying out functions like photosynthesis by the green leaves, transpiration, storage, etc. Under the theoretical information, one activity regarding this was also given which I resolved to perform. Thus, I took a transparent glass from the kitchen, filled it about half with water and mixed the red liquid dye - Alta - in it so as to prepare a coloured solution. However, not upto my expectations, initially there was no visible change within a few hours which made me slightly doubtful. But in the next 1-2 days, something visible gradually began to take place. I noticed that the leaf veins and the midribs have turned faintly reddish indicating that my expectations have been fulfilled. But then another question arose in my mind - why had the textbook mentioned to cut the stem base? To quench my curiosity, I performed the experiment again but this time with two plants — one having its roots intact named plant A, and another having its roots cut from the stem base named plant B. After about a couple of days, as I have seen earlier, plant B showed the reddish colour in its veins and midribs of the leaves. But to my astonishment, plant A did not show such a change quite visibly. So I waited for another 1-2 days and then noticed the leaves of plant A too turn reddish — however the intensity of the colour was clearly less than that of plant B. After searching on the web and asking my science teacher about this observation, I got to know how roots and root hairs selectively absorb and filter the materials entering inside offering restriction to the flow of dye and thus, reducing the intensity of the colour on leaves of plant A; while there was no such filtration process and the coloured water entered directly into the xylem vessels of plant B ensuring faster demonstration of the results. Yes I tried to learn about electromagnetic levitation.
It works by using magnetic fields to create an upward force that exactly cancels out the downward pull of gravity. There are a few different ways this happens in the real world:

Types of Levitation:

Magnetic Repulsion:This is the simplest version. If you take two magnets and point their "North" poles toward each other, they push apart. If the top magnet is light enough and the bottom one is strong enough, the top one will hover.

Maglev Trains: These trains use massive electromagnets to float above the tracks. By removing friction between wheels and rails, they can travel at incredible speeds—over 370 mph (600 km/h).

Superconductors: At very cold temperatures, certain materials can expel magnetic fields entirely (the Meissner Effect), allowing them to "lock" into place and float above a magnet with perfect stability. 

The Challenge of Balance:
While it sounds easy to just point two magnets at each other, there is a catch. If we ever try to hold two magnets in a "pushing" position, we probably noticed they really want to flip over and snap together instead of staying balanced.

Electromagnetism is one of the four fundamental forces of nature. It is the physical interaction that occurs between electrically charged particles. For a long time, I thought that electricity and magnetism were separate forces, but now I know they are inextricably linked.
How it Works:
The core of electromagnetism is the relationship between moving charges and fields:
Electric Fields:Any charged particle creates an electric field that exerts a force on other charges.
Magnetic Fields:When those charged particles move they produce a magnetic field.
Induction: A changing magnetic field can induce an electric current in a nearby conductor. This "handshake" between electricity and magnetism is called electromagnetic induction.
 It is Used:
Our modern world would not function without electromagnetism. It is the basis for:
 Motors and Generators: Converting electrical energy into motion or motion into electricity. Eg dams.
Communication: Our phone, Wi-Fi, and radio all use electromagnetic waves to send data.
Medicine:MRI machines use magnetic fields and radio waves to create detailed images of the inside of the body.

The limitation of words has always fascinated me. In the summer of my sophomore year, I realized that while I could express complex thoughts in English, I was entirely helpless in communicating with my visiting great-grandmother, who speaks only a rural dialect of Vietnamese. My desire to connect with her, to hear the stories of my heritage directly from the source, sparked a quest for a new language. My curiosity drove me to YouTube channels dedicated to language acquisition, and later, to watching old Vietnamese dramas with English subtitles to understand context and emotion.
The real intellectual challenge, however, was the tones. Missing a single diacritic mark could turn "mother" into "ghost." My bedroom became a laboratory for phonetics.
 I recorded myself speaking, comparing my pitch profiles to native speakers, adjusting my tongue and throat positioning until my “nhà” (house) sounded less like “naho” (to release). The frustration was immense, and at times, I wanted to quit. Yet, the thought of conversing with my great-grandmother kept me going. I began keeping a diary entirely in Vietnamese, looking up words I didn't know, turning my confusion into a research project.
Beyond language, this pursuit opened a door to my history. I discovered that Vietnamese phrasing is deeply relational, emphasizing respect for seniority—a concept I had only vaguely understood. I began reading bilingual poetry, trying to grasp the melancholy beauty of Vietnamese literature.

When I finally greeted my great-grandmother with a "Choo cụ" (Hello, Elder) and managed a broken sentence about the weather, her eyes lit up. We spent hours that summer sitting on the porch, her speaking slowly, me listening intently, bridging a gap that had existed my entire life.

According to electrostatics, these protons should push each other apart, making the nucleus unstable. Yet atoms exist in a stable form, suggesting the presence of a force that overcomes this electrostatic repulsion. This force is the strong nuclear force, which acts between nucleons (protons and neutrons). It is extremely powerful but operates only over very short distances, about 1–3 femtometers, allowing it to dominate when nucleons are very close.

The concept of binding energy further explains this phenomenon, as a stable nucleus exists in a lower energy state than its separate particles. However, this balance is delicate, and an improper neutron-to-proton ratio can lead to instability and radioactive decay.
What fascinates me most is how opposing forces coexist to create stability. It shows that at microscopic scales, nature behaves in ways that challenge intuition and motivates me to explore physics more deeply.

In one case, the system kept retrying the same action without making progress, just looping and consuming resources. It wasn’t confused it simply had no way to recognize that it should stop. In another situation, when given a time-sensitive task, it escalated its actions instead of stopping, which made the outcome worse.

These failures made me rethink my approach. Instead of focusing only on making the system “smarter,” I started exploring ideas from control theory, system design, and feedback mechanisms. I didn’t follow a structured path I moved across different concepts, trying to understand why some systems remain stable while others fail under similar conditions.

I also engaged with discussions in a restricted OWASP AI Exchange contributors group, where practitioners analyze real-world risks, failure modes, and constraints in AI systems. Seeing how these issues appear outside small experiments made me realize that these failures are not edge cases, but fundamental limitations of how such systems are currently designed.

To test my understanding, I built a small runtime layer that tracks signals like progress and effort, and enforces stopping conditions. The early versions behaved inconsistently sometimes stopping too early, and other times failing to stop at all. Through repeated iteration, I realized that control mechanisms cannot depend on the system’s reasoning. They must operate independently and enforce limits consistently, regardless of what the system “believes.”

This led me to a broader insight: intelligence and control are separate layers. A system can be capable, yet still behave unstably if there are no constraints governing its actions. Stability does not emerge automatically from intelligence it must be designed into the system.

This also made me think about how such failures scale. In simple experiments, a looping system only wastes time or resources. But in larger, real-world systems, similar behavior could lead to compounding errors, inefficient decisions, or unintended consequences. This reinforced my belief that designing systems that know when to stop is not just an implementation detail, but a fundamental requirement for building reliable autonomous systems.

This experience changed how I approach learning. Instead of relying on predefined paths, I try to understand systems by building, testing, and observing where they fail. I’ve become more comfortable working without clear answers and refining ideas through iteration. More importantly, I’ve learned to question assumptions that seem obvious at first, and to look for underlying principles that explain why systems behave the way they do.

A few summers ago, I noticed my family's potted balcony plants repeatedly wilting because we kept forgetting to water them. Instead of just setting a daily alarm, I decided to build an automated soil-moisture monitoring system. The only problem was that I had zero experience with electronics, microcontrollers, or C++ programming. I was starting entirely from scratch.

I began by scouring the internet, landing on the Arduino platform as the most accessible starting point. I saved up to buy a basic starter kit and spent the first week just trying to make a single LED blink. However, the transition from making a light blink to reading analog sensor data was steep. I quickly fell down a rabbit hole of online forums, documentation, and tutorials. I learned about voltage dividers, analog-to-digital conversion, and the importance of calibrating sensors. My first prototype was a mess of jumper wires on a breadboard. When I finally plugged in the soil moisture sensor and placed it in a cup of water, the serial monitor spit out erratic, nonsensical numbers.

Instead of giving up, I realized I needed to understand the "why" behind the failure. Through patient troubleshooting, I discovered two things: my breadboard connections were loose, and the cheap sensor I bought was prone to rapid corrosion. I learned how to solder to make the connections permanent and rewrote my code to only power the sensor for a fraction of a second during readings to prevent rapid oxidation.

When the system finally worked—lighting up a red LED and sounding a small buzzer only when the soil was genuinely dry—the sense of accomplishment was immense. But the physical device wasn't the most valuable takeaway. This project fundamentally changed how I approach the unknown. It taught me that frustration is an inherent part of the learning curve and that "failure" is just data pointing toward the next iteration. I learned how to break down an intimidating, complex goal into manageable, learnable micro-skills. This self-driven journey sparked my deeper interest in embedded systems and automation, proving to me that with curiosity and determination, no subject is out of reach.

Section G - Essay Curiosity:
During my exploration of buoyancy and the principles behind submarine mechanics, I decided to create a small, fully functional model submarine. The project aimed to demonstrate two primary types of motion: vertical motion (floating and submerging) and horizontal motion (forward and backward propulsion). For the submarine’s hull, I selected a piece of PVC pipe due to its affordability, durability, ease of handling, and wide availability. One end of the pipe was sealed to create a watertight chamber, forming the main body of the submarine.
To control floating and submergence, I implemented the concept of ballast tanks, just like in real submarines. I used thin plastic bottles as ballast tanks because they could be easily emptied or filled with water. These bottles were attached to the hull, and I connected a small submersible water pump to the opening of each bottle, ensuring a tight seal. By turning on the pump to evacuate water from the bottle, the overall density of the submarine decreased, becoming less than the surrounding water. As a result, the submarine floated to the surface. Conversely, when I reversed the pump to fill the bottles with water from the environment, the submarine’s density increased beyond that of water, causing it to submerge.
The first prototype failed because the plastic bottles leaked despite being sealed. After ensuring proper waterproofing, I retested the model, but it still failed to submerge. I realized that the air cavity inside the PVC pipe reduced the overall density too much, even when the ballast tanks were full. To resolve this, I switched to a PVC pipe with a thinner diameter, optimizing the internal volume and making the density adjustments more effective. This design allowed the submarine to successfully float and submerge on command.
For horizontal propulsion, I installed a motor to push the water backward, enabling forward motion via thrust. Initially, the motor lacked sufficient torque, and the submarine barely moved. I upgraded to a high-torque motor, which provided adequate thrust to propel the entire submarine forward and backward smoothly. To enhance the experiment further, I implemented a wireless connection for all electrical controls, eliminating the need for external wires .
Through multiple prototypes, I gained hands-on experience with the practical applications of Archimedes’ principle, fluid mechanics, and propulsion dynamics. This project taught me the importance of careful design iteration, density management, and selecting appropriate motors for specific loads. Although it was a small project i understood the difference between theoretical and practical knowledge .It taught me way more than i expected .
